channel.title: Thirsty Planet
channel.description: Understanding water, before it's gone. The hidden water inside everyday things, the water industry in plain words, and the places already solving it.

item.title: Thirsty: Paper
item.description:
Every office email footer used to beg the same thing: please consider the environment before printing. That request was worth about 10 litres of water per sheet.
Most of it went through a tree. A plantation pine or eucalyptus drinks rain for years before it becomes pulp, and that patience is what the sheet inherits. The mill's share used to be enormous too, but this is one of industry's quiet success stories. A modern paper mill runs its water in loops and uses about a tenth of what mills used decades ago. The machines improved. The tree still takes its time.
The everyday scale is what makes paper interesting. One sheet is nothing. A ream is 5,000 litres. An office printer that runs through a box of paper a week is quietly moving a swimming pool through it every few months. And the recycled sheet in the same tray skips the tree entirely, which roughly halves the whole number.
The long version, with the breakdown and the sources, is on the site.
#WaterFootprint #HiddenWater #Sustainability #Water

item.title: Thirsty Industries: Food and beverage
item.description:
Cook one dinner and look at the sink afterwards. The colander, the pans, the board covered in potato peel, the water going brown in the bowl. That is a food factory, except it never stops and it handles tonnes an hour.
Food and beverage is a bigger industry than most people picture. Dairies, breweries, bottling plants, bakeries, meat plants, canneries, sugar mills. In Europe it is the largest manufacturing sector there is, and one of the heaviest industrial users of water anywhere.
The strange part is that most of that water never touches the food. Somewhere between half and two thirds of it goes on cleaning the equipment. A crisp factory washes its potatoes, steam peels them, slices them, rinses off the starch, fries, cools, and at the end of the shift washes down the whole line. A dairy pushes hot water and detergent through its own pipework between every batch, and in some plants that cleaning uses more water than the milk it processed.
Nobody can simply wash less. When the product is food, hygiene is not a place to economise. So the industry got clever in another direction: water used in order, cleanest job first, dirtiest last, and the sugary, milky effluent at the end digested into biogas that heats the factory.
The long version, with the tables and the sources, is on the site.
#IndustrialWater #WaterTreatment #Sustainability #Water

item.title: Plain Water: Sludge
item.description:
A wastewater plant does not make dirt disappear. Nothing does. What a plant actually does is sort: clean water goes out one way, and everything that was in it gets gathered into a single heap. That heap has a name, sludge, and it is the part of the industry nobody puts on the brochure.
Two things about it surprise people. The first is that fresh sludge is about 99 percent water. The plant then spends enormous effort squeezing it down to a cake that is roughly a quarter solids and still feels damp, so a good deal of the machinery in a treatment works exists to take water out of something that was just taken out of water. The second is the bill. Handling sludge can eat up to half of a plant's running costs.
There is a good story in it too. Digested in sealed tanks, sludge gives off biogas that plants burn for power, and what remains is full of nitrogen and phosphorus, which is exactly what farmland wants. The complication is that everything anyone pours down a drain ends up in the same heap, including the forever chemicals called PFAS, and in 2022 the state of Maine banned spreading sludge on farmland because of them.
The long version is on the site.
#WaterTreatment #Wastewater #WaterEducation #Water

item.title: Thirsty: Milk
item.description:
A litre of milk takes about 1,020 litres of water to produce. As with steak and eggs, the animal barely drinks any of it. The water is in the grass, hay and grain a dairy cow works through every day to keep giving milk.
The question this number always raises is about the alternatives. Counted by irrigation water in one large global study, dairy is the heaviest option per litre. Almond milk comes next, mostly because almonds grow in dry places on pumped water. Oat and soy sit far below both. Different studies count differently, so the figures move around, but the order stays fairly stable.
Worth adding before anyone clears out the fridge: per gram of protein, milk performs about as well as eggs and much better than beef. And a carton from cows grazing rain fed pasture tells a different story than one from a dry region herd eating irrigated feed. The average hides a lot.
The long version, with the tables and the sources, is on the site.
#WaterFootprint #HiddenWater #Sustainability #Water

item.title: Thirsty: Bread
item.description:
Bread rarely makes anyone's list of thirsty foods, which is exactly why it belongs on this one. A kilo of bread carries about 1,608 litres of water. Cut the loaf into slices and each one took roughly 65 litres, about the same as a seven minute shower.
Almost all of it is the wheat. Wheat is the largest crop on the planet by land area, a quiet carpet across Europe, the American plains, India, China and Russia. Around 70 percent of its water arrives as rain, which is the gentle kind. The concern sits in the other 30 percent. In parts of northern India and the Middle East, wheat runs on pumped groundwater, and the wells there have been dropping for decades. Same grain, very different sources.
Bread also makes the multiplication visible. One kilo is manageable. Humanity bakes hundreds of millions of tonnes of wheat into food every year, and every tonne carried its water with it.
The long version, with the breakdown and the sources, is on the site.
#WaterFootprint #HiddenWater #Sustainability #Water

item.title: Plain Water: ETP
item.description:
Next to almost every serious factory in the world there is a building most people never notice. Tanks, pipes, a smell of earth, a low hum. That building decides whether the river next door stays alive.
It is called an ETP, an effluent treatment plant, and inside the industry its nickname is the factory's kidney. Used water comes in carrying dye, oil, starch, salt, whatever the factory does for a living. The plant takes it out. The surprising part is how: the core of nearly every ETP is a large tank of bacteria that eat pollution as food. Operators feed them, keep them warm, and pump air into the water around the clock so they can breathe. Half or more of the plant's electricity goes on that air.
Which points at the real weakness. An ETP costs money every hour it runs and makes nothing anyone can sell. So in places with thin margins and thinner enforcement, plants get switched off between inspections. The technology was solved decades ago. Running it, honestly, every day, is the part the world is still working on.
The long version is on the site.
#WaterTreatment #Wastewater #WaterEducation #Water

item.title: Plain Water: COD
item.description:
A strange fact from the water business: one of the worst things you can pour into a river is milk.
Not because it is toxic. Because of the number the industry uses to measure how dirty water is. It is called COD, chemical oxygen demand, and it is the amount of oxygen it would take to break down everything dissolved in a litre of water. Dirt in water is food. Microbes eat it and breathe oxygen from the water while they do, the same oxygen fish need. COD measures how much oxygen the dirt could take down with it.
A clean mountain stream has a COD of about 2 milligrams per litre. Raw sewage is around 500. Milk is roughly 200,000. A tanker of milk in a river is treated as a serious pollution emergency, and now you know why.
Every discharge permit sets a COD limit. Every treatment plant is judged by how much COD it removes. It is a load meter, not a poison meter, and that distinction is the whole art of reading it.
The long version is on the site.
#WaterTreatment #Wastewater #WaterEducation #Water

item.title: Plain Water: After you flush
item.description:
The flush is the last most people ever see of their water. From there it starts a trip that runs under every street in the city, powered mostly by gravity, all the way to a plant at the lowest point of town.
Two things about that plant surprise almost everyone. First, sewage is about 99.9 percent water. The whole system, the pipes, the tanks, the billions in infrastructure, exists to remove a fraction the size of a sugar cube in a bucket. Second, the plant runs on biology. The cleaning is done by tanks of bacteria that eat the dirt, and the dirt they remove is digested into biogas. The better plants power a large share of their own operations with it, which means a flush partly funds its own cleanup.
The number worth sitting with is global. By UN estimates more than 80 percent of the world's wastewater still returns to nature with no treatment at all. The technology is a century old. Most of humanity just does not have the plant yet.
The long version is on the site.
#WaterTreatment #Wastewater #WaterEducation #Water

item.title: Thirsty: Rice
item.description:
A flooded rice paddy looks like the crop must need to grow underwater. It does not. Rice grows fine in moist soil. The water is there mostly as weed control: rice tolerates standing water and weeds drown in it. Farmers have used that trick for thousands of years because it works and needs no chemicals.
The cost of the trick is scale. Rice feeds about half the world every day, and growing one kilo takes around 2,500 litres of water. Across Asia's paddies that adds up to roughly a third of all the irrigation water used on Earth, more than any other crop.
The interesting part is happening on farms right now. A method called alternate wetting and drying, where paddies are allowed to dry out for a few days before being flooded again, cuts water use by about a quarter without losing yield. It is low tech, it is spreading, and it is one of the biggest single water savings available anywhere.
The long version, with the numbers and the sources, is on the site.
#WaterFootprint #HiddenWater #Sustainability #Water

item.title: Thirsty: Chocolate
item.description:
A 100 gram bar of chocolate takes about 1,700 litres of water to produce. Most people read that number twice.
The explanation is mostly the tree. Cocoa grows in the wettest parts of Ghana, Ivory Coast and Indonesia, drinks rain all year, and at the end of a season a single tree yields only a few kilos of beans. Then it takes a lot of beans to make a little chocolate. So each bar carries years of accumulated rainfall, around 17,000 litres per kilo, which on paper is more than beef.
Worth knowing before drawing conclusions: about 98 percent of that water is rain that fell on tropical farmland anyway. Cocoa is not draining rivers. Its actual problem is temperature. The belt where cocoa grows well keeps getting narrower as the climate warms, and the industry is already moving farms and breeding for heat because of it.
The long version, with the breakdown and the sources, is on the site.
#WaterFootprint #HiddenWater #Sustainability #Water

item.title: Thirsty: Beef
item.description:
A 200 gram steak carries about 3,100 litres of water, and nearly all of it was spent before the animal ever drank.
Cattle eat for roughly three years before slaughter: grass, hay, grain. Growing all that feed takes water every season, and when those years of feed water are divided by the meat one animal yields, beef lands around 15,400 litres per kilo, the highest of the common meats. The animal's own drinking water is about one percent of the total.
The number changes a great deal with how the animal was raised. Cattle on rain fed pasture mostly use rain that fell on grassland anyway. Cattle fed irrigated grain in a dry region draw on rivers and aquifers. The same steak on the plate, a very different water story behind it.
The long version, with the breakdown and the sources, is on the site.
#WaterFootprint #HiddenWater #Sustainability #Water

item.title: The turn
item.description:
Every number posted in the first month of this series was spent before the product reached anyone. Coffee, 140 litres. A t-shirt, 2,700. A steak, 3,100. Jeans, 8,000. Read enough of those and it starts to feel like a personal accusation. It is not one.
Those litres were used in fields and factories, and factory water in particular has a property that changes everything: it is concentrated. A mill's wastewater leaves through one pipe, and whatever flows through one pipe can be measured, treated and sent back into the process. With equipment that already exists, 70 to 90 percent of industrial wastewater can be recovered. Plants doing exactly this run every day, quietly, on every continent.
The reason it is not standard everywhere is rarely technical: cost, and whether customers, regulators or neighbours are asking for it. Asking turns out to matter.
This is where the series turns: less "look how much water", more "look what can be done with it".
The long version is on the site.
#WaterFootprint #WaterEducation #Sustainability #Water

item.title: Thirsty: T-shirt
item.description:
There is a sea missing in Central Asia, and part of the reason is hanging in your wardrobe.
The Aral Sea was once the fourth largest lake on Earth. From the 1960s the two rivers feeding it were diverted to irrigate cotton, and over a few decades most of it turned to desert. Fishing towns now sit a hundred kilometres from the water.
That is the uncomfortable thing about cotton. It is a natural fibre, it feels like the responsible choice, and it is also one of the thirstiest crops in farming. One t-shirt carries about 2,700 litres of water by the Water Footprint Network's method, roughly what one person drinks in three years. About 85 percent of it is the field.
The good news does not require shopping differently. It mostly requires keeping clothes longer. Every extra year a shirt stays in use, its water per wear shrinks.
The long version, with the breakdown and the sources, is on the site.
#WaterFootprint #HiddenWater #Sustainability #Water

item.title: Thirsty: Jeans
item.description:
The CEO of Levi's once told an audience he had not washed his jeans in a year. It sounded like a stunt. It was actually water policy.
His company had just finished one of the most detailed studies ever done on a single garment, and it found something unexpected: nearly a quarter of all the water a pair of jeans uses in its lifetime is spent in the owner's washing machine. The farm grows the cotton, the mill dyes it blue, and then the biggest saving left on the table belongs to whoever wears them.
The full farm to shop number is about 8,000 litres per pair, by the Water Footprint Network's method. Around 85 percent of it is the cotton field. The dye house, where the colour goes on and a good part of it comes straight back off in the rinse, is a distant second.
The long version, with the breakdown, the indigo chemistry and the sources, is on the site.
#WaterFootprint #HiddenWater #Sustainability #Water

item.title: Thirsty Industries: Textile
item.description:
Fashion withdraws 93 billion cubic metres of water a year. Almost all of it comes back, and that is the problem.
Textiles is an industry that consumes little water and discharges a lot of it: hot, alkaline, loaded with salt, and coloured by dye that never bonded to the fibre. Colour is the part people underestimate. Dye blocks light from reaching into a river, less light means less photosynthesis, and less photosynthesis means less oxygen for anything living in it.
I have stood inside the plants that deal with this water. Conventional wet processing uses 100 to 150 litres of water per kilo of fabric. The best run mills operate near 50, and the gap between those numbers is management, not new technology. Beyond that, a treatment plant followed by membranes can bring 70 to 90 percent of a mill's effluent back into the process.
Treatment does not make the pollution disappear, though. It concentrates it into two streams, a salty brine and a heap of sludge, and what a mill does with those two is now the real question in this industry.
The long version, with the effluent table, the dye house mechanism and the sources, is on the site.
#IndustrialWater #WaterTreatment #Sustainability #Water

item.title: Thirsty: Coffee
item.description:
By the time a cup of coffee reaches your kitchen, about 140 litres of water have already gone into it. The kettle adds a fraction of a litre. The rest was spent months earlier, on a hillside in Ethiopia, Brazil or Vietnam, while the beans were still on the tree.
The number comes from the Water Footprint Network method, which counts three kinds of water: the rain the crop drank, the irrigation it was given, and the water needed to dilute whatever it polluted. Per kilo of roasted coffee it comes to roughly 18,900 litres. A cup uses about seven grams, so 132 litres for the growing, a few more for processing, and the cup is done.
The part most people never hear is that a big number is not automatically bad news. Most coffee grows on rain, and rain on a tropical hillside was never going to come out of anyone's tap. The story changes when thirsty crops are grown in dry places on pumped water. So the useful question about coffee, and about most things you own, is whose water it was, and where it came from.
The full article, with the breakdown, the mechanism and the sources, is on the site.
#WaterFootprint #HiddenWater #Sustainability #Water

item.title: The 0.3%
item.description:
Somewhere in school, everyone saw the photo of Earth from space and heard that 70 percent of the planet is water. True, and it hides the real story.
About 97.5 percent of Earth's water is salt. Of the small fraction that is fresh, most is frozen in ice sheets and glaciers or lies too deep underground to reach. The rivers and lakes that supply most of what people, farms and factories actually use hold about 0.3 percent of the freshwater, which is less than a hundredth of a percent of all the water on the planet.
The twist is that this small share never runs out. Rain brings it back every year. So why do cities go dry? Because water is the one resource that cannot be shipped around the planet. Oil goes on a tanker. A river stays where it is. One country has more than it knows what to do with, and another counts the days until the taps stop.
That is the story this series tells, one everyday object at a time. The long version is on the site.
#WaterFootprint #WaterEducation #Sustainability #Water

item.title: Thirsty Places: Singapore
item.description:
Singapore has almost no natural freshwater. So it built a national supply out of the water it had already used.
The country runs what it calls four national taps: rain caught across the island, water imported from Malaysia, desalinated seawater, and NEWater, which is treated used water clean enough to drink and able to meet up to 40 percent of national demand.
NEWater is microfiltration, then reverse osmosis, then ultraviolet disinfection. None of that is exotic. It is standard equipment, the same train a textile mill uses to recycle its effluent, run well and maintained properly. The engineering was the easy part.
Asking people to drink it took more work, and Singapore did it by showing the process instead of hiding it. Years of published testing before launch. A visitor centre where the membranes are behind glass. A prime minister drinking it on camera. A name that described the product rather than its past.
Most cities that have rejected water reuse had the same technology available. What they lacked was that conversation.
The long version, with the four taps, the process and the sources, is on the site.
#WaterScarcity #WaterManagement #Cities #Water

item.title: Thirsty: Beer
item.description:
How much water does it take to make a beer? Not the water in the glass. All of it: the barley in the field, the rain and irrigation months before the brewery, the brewing itself.
One 250 millilitre glass comes to about 74 litres by the Water Footprint Network's method, roughly 298 litres for every litre of beer. Around 92 percent of it grew the barley. The brewery is a rounding error on top.
The part I find genuinely hopeful is inside that rounding error. Making one litre of beer takes around four to seven litres of water in a conventional brewery, most of it for cleaning tanks and pipes between batches, and the best operations have pushed the figure below three. Brewing is one of the industries that measures its water hardest, because every litre saved is money, and the effluent, rich in sugar and yeast, is increasingly digested for biogas.
Same story as coffee. The water is real, it was just spent somewhere else.
The long version, with the breakdown and the sources, is on the site.
#WaterFootprint #HiddenWater #Sustainability #Water

item.title: Plain Water: Wastewater
item.description:
Wastewater is not a dirty word, and it is not another word for sewage.
It is any water that has already been used, by a shower, a brewery, a farm, a street in the rain, and now carries something it did not carry before. Sewage is one kind of it. A factory's effluent is another. Runoff is a third. Using the words interchangeably is the most common mistake people make about my industry.
The part that surprises people: typical municipal wastewater is more than 99 percent plain water. The whole business of treatment exists for the last one percent, and that one percent is enough. Bacteria in a river eat the organic matter in it and use up the dissolved oxygen while they do. Fish suffocate long before the water ever looks dirty.
Almost nothing in wastewater is visible. It is dissolved. That is why the sector measures water rather than looking at it, and why the next terms in this series are all measurements.
The long version is on the site.
#WaterTreatment #Wastewater #WaterEducation #Water

item.title: Myth: Bottled water is cleaner than tap
item.description:
"Bottled water is cleaner than tap." It depends, but not for the reason most people assume.
In most of Europe, tap water is held to a public health standard and monitored continuously across the whole network, from the plant to the street. Bottled water is held to a product standard and tested batch by batch at the factory. The rules for bottled water ask for consistency, batch after batch, rather than for a higher purity than tap.
Two points are usually reversed. First, "natural mineral water" describes where the water came from and how stable it is, and the law forbids disinfecting it. It is allowed to keep minerals a treatment plant would remove, and sells them as a feature. Second, the chlorine smell people dislike is a deliberate trace of disinfectant that stops anything regrowing in the pipes on the way to your tap. Bottled water has no such protection, which is why an opened bottle left warm in a car is the worse container of the two.
The honest nuance: where the mains supply is unreliable, a boil notice is in force, or the plumbing is old, bottled genuinely is the safer call. Context decides it, not the packaging.
The long version, with the two rulebooks and the sources, is on the site.
#WaterFacts #WaterEducation #Sustainability #Water

item.title: Plain Water: Microplastics
item.description:
A study in 2024 counted the plastic in a litre of bottled water with a new laser technique and found about 240,000 pieces, ninety percent of them smaller than a micron. Earlier counts, which could only see the larger particles, had found a few hundred. The plastic was there all along. The instruments caught up.
Microplastics are in rivers, rain, the sea, the deep ocean, the air of a living room, and the blood and placentas of people who have been tested. They come from tyres wearing on roads, synthetic clothes shedding in the wash, paint, packaging, and the breakdown of everything plastic that was ever thrown away. They reach water through the sewage works, which removes most of them and sends them to the sludge, and from there to the fields.
What is known: they are everywhere and the counts rise with every better instrument. What is unknown: what they do to a body at the doses found. What is certain: a conventional treatment plant takes out most of them, and bottled water carries more than a tap. The one place where the answer is easy is the one most people get wrong.
The long version is on the site.
#WaterTreatment #Wastewater #WaterEducation #Water

item.title: Thirsty: Roses
item.description:
A rose stem from a Kenyan farm carries about ten litres of water, and there are twenty in a bunch. The flower is grown under plastic on the shore of Lake Naivasha, a freshwater lake in the Rift Valley a hundred kilometres from Nairobi, cut in the morning, chilled, packed, trucked to the airport that evening, flown to Amsterdam overnight, auctioned by lunchtime and on a shelf in London or Berlin the next day. Kenya sends Europe about a third of its roses, and most of them come from one lake.
The industry moved to the equator because the light is constant, the labour is cheap, and a greenhouse at 1,900 metres needs no heating, so that a Kenyan rose, flown, carries less carbon than a Dutch one grown under lamps in February. The water is the lake's. Naivasha fell by several metres in the 2000s as the farms drew on it and the rains failed, and the fish, the hippos and the town that drew on it too found the shore a kilometre away. It has since risen with the rains, and the farms have moved to drip and to recycling because the buyers asked.
A rose is water, air freight and a week in a vase. The water is the part that stays in Kenya.
The long version is on the site.
#WaterFootprint #HiddenWater #Sustainability #Water

item.title: Thirsty Places: Los Angeles
item.description:
Los Angeles gets about 380 millimetres of rain a year and has a river that runs in a concrete channel and is dry for most of it. The city exists because in 1913 it opened an aqueduct three hundred and seventy five kilometres long from the Owens valley on the far side of the Sierra Nevada, having bought the valley's water rights through agents who did not say who they worked for, and because it then reached for the Colorado in 1941 and the rivers of northern California in 1972. Every drop it drinks is imported, and every source it imports from is shrinking.
The Owens valley became a dust bowl; the lake the aqueduct drained was, for decades, the largest source of dust pollution in the United States, and the city now spends more water keeping the dust down than it takes. The Colorado, which supplies a quarter of southern California, is in its longest drought in a thousand years, and the states that share it are negotiating who loses.
The city's answer is the one Orange County and Singapore gave: recycle. The largest sewage works on the coast is being rebuilt to turn all of its outflow into drinking water by 2035, which would give the city a third of its supply from inside its own borders for the first time in a century.
The long version is on the site.
#WaterScarcity #WaterManagement #Cities #Water

item.title: Thirsty Places: Kathmandu
item.description:
Nepal has the Himalaya, eight of the world's ten highest mountains, and more fresh water per person than almost any country. Its capital gets water a few hours a week. The Kathmandu valley holds four million people in a bowl of hills, the rivers that drain it are small and, below the city, sewers, and the utility's supply in the dry season is about a third of what the valley uses. The rest comes from wells, most of them illegal, and from tankers that queue at the wells at dawn.
The answer was Melamchi: a river in the next valley, a tunnel twenty six kilometres through the hills, and a treatment works on the city's edge. It was designed in the 1980s, financed in 1998, and finished in 2021, after two decades of contractors leaving, a civil war, an earthquake and a political fight over every kilometre. Water flowed in March 2021. In June a flood on the Melamchi buried the intake under metres of debris, and the tunnel has run only in the dry months since.
The valley's wells, meanwhile, have fallen by tens of metres, the stone spouts that watered the old city for a thousand years have dried, and the tankers charge by the litre.
The long version is on the site.
#WaterScarcity #WaterManagement #Cities #Water

item.title: Thirsty Places: Amman
item.description:
In Amman the water comes one day a week. Every district has a delivery day, the pipes are pressurised for it, the tanks on every roof fill, and the household lives from the tank until the next delivery. It has been the system since the 1980s, it is how a city of four million lives in a country with about a hundred cubic metres of water a person a year, a tenth of the level the United Nations calls scarcity, and it is why every building in the city has a row of black tanks on its roof.
The water comes from wells around the city that are falling, from the King Abdullah canal that carries the Yarmouk and the Jordan's tributaries down the valley and pumps them a thousand metres up to the plateau, and, since 2013, from Disi: a fossil aquifer under the southern desert, three hundred kilometres away, tapped by fifty five wells and piped north at a hundred million cubic metres a year. The water fell as rain thirty thousand years ago. When it is used it will not come back.
About half of what enters the pipes is lost or taken without payment. A million Syrian refugees since 2011 added a fifth to the demand. The next source is the sea, at Aqaba, pumped up the length of the country.
The long version is on the site.
#WaterScarcity #WaterManagement #Cities #Water

item.title: Thirsty: Pasta
item.description:
A kilogram of dry pasta carries about 1,850 litres of water, and about 1,800 of them fell as rain on a field of durum wheat, in southern Italy, in Canada, in the American plains or in Kazakhstan. Durum is the hard wheat of dry country, sown where the summers are hot and the rain is scarce, and it is grown almost entirely without irrigation. The bread article on this site does the arithmetic for soft wheat; pasta's is the same, on a harder grain, with less of it eaten per meal.
Italy makes a third of the world's pasta and grows about half the durum it needs; the rest comes from Canada, whose prairies grow more of it than any country, and the water in a bowl of spaghetti in Rome is, for that share, rain on Saskatchewan. The factory adds almost nothing: a few litres a kilogram to mix and dry.
The pot adds the most that a cook ever adds to any food's footprint. The instruction on the packet, a litre of water for every hundred grams, is ten litres a kilogram, heated to the boil and poured down the sink, and the argument in Italy in 2022 about whether a Nobel laureate was right to say the pasta should be cooked with the lid on and the heat off was, at bottom, about that pot.
The long version is on the site.
#WaterFootprint #HiddenWater #Sustainability #Water

item.title: Thirsty Industries: Ski Resorts
item.description:
The snow on most pistes in the Alps was made. Ninety percent of Italy's ski slopes and about seventy percent of Austria's are covered by artificial snow for at least part of the season, blown from cannons and lances on cold nights from water pumped out of reservoirs dug into the high pasture for the purpose. A cubic metre of water makes about two cubic metres of snow, a kilometre of piste takes several thousand cubic metres a season, and a large resort uses the water of a town of ten thousand people between November and March.
The water is not lost, mostly. It melts in spring and runs down the same streams it was pumped from, minus the share that evaporated in the making, which is a fifth to a third. What it is, is moved: taken from the streams in autumn when they are lowest, stored above the treeline in reservoirs that did not exist thirty years ago, and put back in April. The trout in the stream notice. So does the village below the reservoir if the dam fails.
The industry makes snow because the natural kind is failing at the altitudes where the resorts were built, and the snowmaking that keeps a resort open at 1,500 metres in a warm winter is also the reason it is still there to argue about.
The long version is on the site.
#IndustrialWater #WaterTreatment #Sustainability #Water

item.title: Thirsty Industries: Car Washes
item.description:
A car washed with a hose on the drive uses three to five hundred litres of water, and every litre of it, with the soap, the road grime, the brake dust and the oil, runs into the gutter and down a storm drain that leads, in most cities, straight to the river. A car washed in a modern commercial tunnel uses about a hundred and fifty litres of fresh water, because most of what touches the car has been used before, and the water that leaves goes to the sewer and the treatment works.
The industry likes to say this, and it is true. It is also the reason the car wash is the first business to be closed in a drought, because it is visible, it uses water for something nobody needs, and a city that has told its residents to stop watering the lawn cannot leave a tunnel wash running on the main road. The bans that followed the droughts in California, Cape Town and Sydney closed the washes that had spent most on reclaim and left the drive and the bucket, which use more.
The water in the car wash is small. The argument about it is the argument every dry city has in August about what water is for.
The long version is on the site.
#IndustrialWater #WaterTreatment #Sustainability #Water

item.title: Plain Water: Rainwater Harvesting
item.description:
A roof of a hundred square metres in a place with six hundred millimetres of rain a year catches about sixty thousand litres, and after the first flush, the overflow and the evaporation it delivers about forty eight thousand to a tank. That is close to what a careful household of two or three uses indoors in a year, and in most of the world it runs off the roof into a downpipe and a drain and is gone.
Harvesting it is the oldest water technology there is and the least used in cities. Bermuda, which has no rivers, has required every house to catch its roof water since the seventeenth century, and the island's stepped white roofs are the catchment. Chennai made tanks compulsory on every building in 2003 after a drought, and its aquifer rose. About a quarter of Australian households have a tank, most fitted since the Millennium Drought, and in Adelaide it is half.
The water is clean enough for the garden, the toilet and the washing machine without treatment, and for drinking with a filter and a lamp. The tank is the cost. The roof is already there.
The long version is on the site.

item.title: Plain Water: Ballast Water
item.description:
A ship that has unloaded its cargo is too light to sail safely, so it fills tanks in its hull with seawater, tens of thousands of tonnes of it, and carries the water to the port where it loads, where it pumps the water out to make room for the cargo. The world's fleet moves about five billion tonnes of water this way every year, from one sea to another, and every tonne carries whatever was in the water where it was taken on: larvae, algae, bacteria, the eggs of fish, the spores of things that had never been on the other side of an ocean.
The zebra mussel reached the Great Lakes from the Caspian in a ship's tanks in the 1980s and now coats every intake pipe and every boat hull in the basin at a cost of hundreds of millions a year. A comb jelly from the American coast reached the Black Sea the same way and ate the plankton and the fish eggs until the anchovy fishery collapsed. The list runs to hundreds of species and every ocean.
The convention that requires ships to treat their ballast before discharge was agreed in 2004 and came into force in 2017, and a ship now carries, below its waterline, a small water treatment works.
The long version is on the site.

item.title: Myth: A Swimming Pool Wastes More Water Than a Lawn
item.description:
In a drought, the pool is the thing the neighbours point at. It is a tank of drinking water in the garden, it evaporates all summer, and it looks like waste. The lawn next to it, which is what the pool usually replaced, does not look like anything, and in the dry cities where both are common it uses more.
An uncovered pool in Phoenix, Perth or Los Angeles loses about a metre and a half of water a year to evaporation, plus what splashes out and what is drained for cleaning. A lawn of the same area in the same climate needs about a metre and a half to two metres of sprinkler water a year to stay green, every year, and it does not come back when the season ends. The pool is filled once, and topped up. The studies that have metered both, in Phoenix and in Perth, found the pool using the same or less than the grass it sits where.
A cover cuts the pool's evaporation by more than half. Gravel and native planting cut the lawn's water to nothing. The myth is that the pool is the waste; the honest comparison is either of them against a garden that needs no hose.
The long version is on the site.

item.title: Thirsty: Soy
item.description:
A kilogram of soybeans carries about 2,100 litres of water, and about 95 percent of it is rain. Soy is the least irrigated of the world's great crops, grown on the summer rain of the American midwest, the Brazilian plateau and the Argentine pampas, and its footprint is green in the sense the wool and sunflower articles on this site use: water that fell on farmland and would have grown something else.
Very little of it is eaten as soy. About three quarters of the world's crop is crushed for oil and the protein meal that is left goes into the feed of pigs, chickens and farmed fish, so that most of the soy on Earth is eaten as a chicken breast or a pork chop. Tofu, soy milk, tempeh and sauce take about seven percent. A kilogram of tofu carries about 2,500 litres and replaces a kilogram of chicken at 4,300 or beef at 15,000, and a litre of soy milk carries about 300 against a cow's 1,000.
The argument about soy is about land. The crop has spread across the Cerrado, the savanna of central Brazil, faster than any crop in history, and the water it carries is the rain that fell on what was there before.
The long version is on the site.

item.title: Thirsty Places: Santiago
item.description:
Santiago has been in drought since 2010. Central Chile has had a run of dry years longer than anything in its record, with rainfall a third below normal and, more important, a snowpack in the Andes that has shrunk to a fraction, because the snow is what feeds the Maipo river through the dry summer, and the Maipo is where seven million people's water comes from.
Chile is also the country where water is most completely private. The water code of 1981 made rights to water a property separate from the land, granted in perpetuity and freely traded, and the rights to most of the country's rivers were allocated in the 1980s and 1990s to farms, mines and utilities, on the assumption that the rivers would carry what they had. They do not, and the rights add up to more water than exists. A lake south of the city, Aculeo, twelve square kilometres of water with houses and boats on it, dried completely in 2018 while the rights to the streams that fed it were still being exercised upstream.
In 2022 the city's governor announced a rationing plan, the first in its history. The rain that winter was better. The drought has not ended.
The long version is on the site.

item.title: Thirsty Places: Manila
item.description:
Manila drinks from one dam. The Angat reservoir, in the mountains sixty kilometres north east, supplies about ninety seven percent of the water for fourteen million people, and in a year when the rains fail it falls to the level at which the city's two water companies start turning off districts by rota. In March 2019 that happened to the eastern half of the city for weeks, with queues at fire hydrants and hospitals on tankers, while the reservoir that was supposed to take the strain, a second source planned since the 2000s, was still unbuilt.
The city is also the world's largest experiment in private water. In 1997 the state utility, which had lost two thirds of its water to leaks and theft and reached about two thirds of the city, was split into two concessions and sold. One of them cut its losses from sixty three percent to under ten, connected the slums it had been told could not be connected, and became the industry's model. The other took longer. Neither could build a dam.
The dam is now being built, in the Sierra Madre, over the objections of the people whose land it floods, and it will give the city one more source in a country of typhoons and a dry season that is getting longer.
The long version is on the site.

item.title: Thirsty Places: Lahore
item.description:
Lahore is the second city of Pakistan and it drinks entirely from the ground. Every litre its utility supplies comes from more than five hundred deep wells sunk into the sand of the Punjab plain, and the water table under the city has been falling by close to a metre a year for thirty years. It was a few metres down in the 1960s. It is forty to fifty in the centre now.
The reason is the Ravi. The river that the city was built beside was allocated to India by the Indus Waters Treaty of 1960, which divided the rivers of the Punjab between the two countries, and India uses it upstream. What reaches Lahore for most of the year is the city's own sewage and the effluent of its factories, in a channel that was a river, and the city has never built a plant to treat it, because there is nothing in it to treat.
The wells are running into arsenic, as the delta's wells did in Bangladesh, and into the salt that the plain's irrigation left in the ground. The plan to replace them is a canal from the Indus system and a treatment plant, and a new city, built on the dry riverbed, that would need more water than the old one.
The long version is on the site.

item.title: Thirsty: Olive Oil
item.description:
A litre of olive oil carries about fourteen thousand litres of water, twice sunflower oil and three times rapeseed, and for most of the tree's history nearly all of it was rain. The olive is the tree of dry country: it grows on stony hillsides with four hundred millimetres of rain a year, sends its roots deep, and gives a small crop of fruit every year and a larger one every other. The number is high because the yield is low, and the rain was falling on the hillside anyway.
That is changing. Half the world's olive oil is Spanish, most of it from Andalusia, and the groves planted since the 1990s are irrigated: hedgerows of small trees at two thousand to the hectare, watered by drip from the Guadalquivir and from wells, giving several times the yield of the old groves at a cost of a few thousand cubic metres of water per hectare in the driest region of Europe. The old groves carry rain. The new ones carry a river.
In 2022 and 2023 the rain failed in Andalusia and the harvest halved, twice. The world price of olive oil tripled, supermarkets in Spain locked the bottles, and the argument about who the Guadalquivir is for had olive oil in it for the first time.
The long version is on the site.

item.title: Thirsty Industries: Breweries
item.description:
A brewery uses about three litres of water for every litre of beer, and the best plants in the world are under two and a half. A generation ago it was six or seven. The beer article on this site counts the whole footprint of a glass, and the barley is nearly all of it; this one is about the plant, where the water is the process, the cleaning and the cooling, and where the effluent is a sweet, warm, oxygen hungry stream that a sewage works charges extra to take.
The industry counts its water more carefully than most, because a brewery is a large, visible user in a town, and because the largest brewers have learned what a shortage does to a licence. In 2020 the city of Mexicali, in the desert of Baja California, voted by three to one against a nearly finished brewery that would have used twenty million litres a day of the city's groundwater to make beer for export to the United States, and the plant was abandoned with the tanks in place.
The lesson the brewers drew was that the three litres in the plant are the ones that decide whether the plant exists.
The long version is on the site.

item.title: Thirsty Industries: Bottled Water Plants
item.description:
A bottled water plant is a well with a filling line on top. It pumps a spring or an aquifer, filters the water, treats it lightly or not at all, fills it into bottles it usually makes on site from pellets of plastic, and ships it away by truck, which is the one thing that makes it different from every other water user in the town: the water does not come back. A brewery's water returns as effluent, a farm's as drainage and rain. A bottling plant's leaves the watershed in a lorry.
The volumes are small by the standards of this site. The plant at the centre of the long fight in Michigan was permitted for about two million litres a day, the water of a town of ten thousand people, and paid the state two hundred dollars a year for the paperwork. The fight was about the price, the principle and the spring, in that order, and it ran for twenty years through the courts and the state legislature, in a state that sits on a fifth of the world's fresh surface water.
The water is not the point. The bottled water article on this site makes that case. The plant is the point, because it is where a public thing becomes a private one, a few hundred million litres at a time.
The long version is on the site.

item.title: Plain Water: Water Meters
item.description:
When a water meter is fitted to a house that has never had one, the household's use falls by about fifteen percent, and stays down. Nobody in the house was asked to do anything. The bill that used to be a fixed charge, based on the value of the house, became a number that moved with the tap, and the tap moved.
About half the households in England still have no meter, and pay a flat charge whatever they use, which is the arrangement most of the world's cities began with and many of the poorest still have. The utility that cannot see how much each customer uses cannot find the leaks on their side of the pipe, cannot price the pool differently from the kettle, and cannot tell a household that its use has doubled since Tuesday, which is what a burst pipe under the floor looks like.
A smart meter does all three. The catch is the bill, which rises for the large household in the small house, and the politics, which in Ireland in 2016 ended the charges altogether after two years of protests.
The long version is on the site.
